description: Sawissi Lab is led by Mohamed Sawissi, a freelance web and AI developer from Libya. We plan to build a bilingual (Arabic/English) web tool that harmonizes NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspots into one consistent burning activity calendar, so emergency managers and communities, including those around Libya's Green Mountain forests, can see historical fire patterns and unusual activity in any area.
summary: In August 2021 wildfires in Kabylie, Algeria, killed at least 65 people. Was that month exceptional? The satellite record should answer, but it is broken in two: MODIS has mapped fire since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, and VIIRS sees far more small fires, so together they show a jump in 2012 that never happened. Nar Calendar ("nar" is Arabic for fire) joins them into one consistent record, and it answers: August 2021 in Kabylie burned 7 times more than a normal August, the second worst month in 26 years. Pick or draw any area in 13 Mediterranean and North African countries and choose your years: the app builds a burning calendar for every month from November 2000 to October 2026, compares each month with normal, finds the fire season, the record years and the long-term trend, and lets you download the data and the calendar image. It first removes hot spots that are not fires: in Libya, our home, 98 % of satellite hot spots are gas flares and industry. It then tests two conversion methods on your own area by hiding years and predicting them, uses the better one, and shows the measured error (5 % for Italy, 7 % for Algeria, 19 % for Libya). An optional AI analyst explains the numbers in plain English or Arabic. Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026; Nar Calendar already continues the record on NOAA-20.
details:
WHY WE BUILT IT

On 11 August 2021 NASA's Suomi NPP satellite photographed the smoke of the Kabylie fires in Algeria (the opening image of our demo). Algerian state television reported at least 65 dead, 28 of them soldiers sent to fight the flames. Was that month exceptional, or is it the new normal? Nobody could answer from the satellite record, because the record changes instruments in 2012. In Nar Calendar the answer takes one click: August 2021 in Kabylie had 1,201 burning cell-days, 7 times a normal August (169) and the second highest month since 2000; only August 2012 was higher (1,703). The same question can now be asked for any place in 13 countries.

WHAT IS NEW HERE

1. Gas flares as a satellite heartbeat. Gas flares burn every day, so a day on which a sensor reports no hot spot of any kind over three flare-rich countries is a satellite outage, not a quiet day. This simple test finds outage days from the data itself and lets the app correct the affected months.

2. A harmonization that grades itself. For the exact area the user draws, the app hides each year, predicts it, chooses the better of two methods and shows its own error, or says that the area has too few fires to be trusted.

3. The record did not stop when the satellite did. Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026; NOAA-20 is already joined, with the same self-test.

WHAT IT DOES

Nar Calendar is a web application: https://nar.vorelq.com (code: https://github.com/ayanmohamedali7-blip/nar-calendar). The user chooses a country, then a ready-made area, a drawn rectangle or polygon, or typed latitude and longitude, and a range of years. The app returns a burning calendar (month by year, November 2000 to October 2026) in one unit, a view that ranks each month against the same month of other years, the latest month against its historical median, the fire season, the most active years and months, the long-term trend, and a chart of raw MODIS, raw VIIRS and the harmonized record with a likely range for the older years. Everything can be downloaded: the monthly series and every fire cell as CSV, and the calendar as a PNG image. A link reopens the exact area, years and month.

HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

1. Real fires only. From NASA FIRMS we keep detections labelled as presumed vegetation fire and drop low-confidence ones. We then mask every 1 km cell around a known static heat source and every place that is hot all year round. In Libya this keeps 12,605 of 737,948 hot spots (1.7 %). The FIRMS type label alone is not enough: about 80 % of detections labelled "vegetation fire" in Libya sit right next to gas flares.

2. One unit. Both sensors go on the same 0.01 degree grid. A cell with at least one detection on a day counts once: a burning cell-day. This removes the pixel-size difference (375 m against 1 km).

3. Satellite outages. A satellite that is down for ten days makes a month look quiet. We detect every day on which a sensor delivered no hot spot of any kind across three countries full of gas flares (flares burn daily, so such a day is an outage, for example Suomi NPP from 27 July to 10 August 2022) and scale those months to a full month.

4. Two methods, tested on the user's own area. For 2012 to 2026 both sensors watched the same land. Rank matching (quantile mapping) converts a MODIS month to the VIIRS value of the same rank; monthly conversion factors scale it. Each year of 2012 to 2026 is hidden in turn and predicted from MODIS alone, and the method with the smaller error is used. The app shows that error and names the method.

5. One record. Before February 2012 the calendar shows converted MODIS, afterwards VIIRS as observed.

6. The record goes on after Suomi NPP. The same instrument flies on NOAA-20 (in FIRMS since April 2018). Its detections pass the same filters and are converted to Suomi NPP units, and the conversion is tested the same way: each year of 2018 to 2026 is hidden and predicted from NOAA-20 alone. Typical miss of a yearly total for whole countries: Turkey 2 %; Spain, Italy, Algeria and Egypt 3 %; Greece and Syria 4 %; Morocco 5 %; Portugal 7 %; Tunisia 8 %; Libya and Lebanon 10 %; Cyprus, with few fires, 20 %. NOAA-20 already supplies the eight months since 2018 in which Suomi NPP was down for three days or more, and the app shows the month in progress from NOAA-20 alone. The MODIS and Suomi NPP record is not changed by this step.

WHAT WE LEARNED

VIIRS reports about 9 times more burning cells than MODIS in Libya, 3.5 times in the Jebel Akhdar forests and 13 times on the Jefara farmland, so a single factor cannot work. No method is best everywhere: rank matching wins by a wide margin where MODIS misses most fires (North Africa), monthly factors are sometimes better where large forest fires dominate (Galicia, northern Portugal). Measured error of a yearly total for whole countries: Italy 5 %, Spain 6 %, Algeria 7 %, Portugal 7 %, Greece 8 %, Turkey 9 %, Morocco 10 %, Libya 19 %, Egypt 28 %. The record matches events people remember: the Kabylie fires of August 2021, Algeria's 2012 season, the autumn rice-straw burning of the Nile Delta. Galicia shows a significant falling trend.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW

Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, after a year of growing outages that our outage detector picked up. The fire record had to be joined again, and Nar Calendar already does it: NOAA-20 is joined with the same tested method (step 6), and NOAA-21 is next. Civil protection and forest services can see when their season really starts and whether this month is abnormal; researchers get a 26-year series with its uncertainty; countries with gas flaring get a fire record that is not polluted by industry.

AI ANALYST

A button asks an open-weight language model (Llama 3.3 on Cloudflare Workers AI) to explain the statistics of the selected area in plain English or Arabic, or to answer one question. The model receives only the numbers the app already computed, is instructed to use nothing else, and its text is labelled as AI-generated. If it is unreachable, the app writes a summary by code.

LIMITS

Satellites miss fires under cloud and between overpasses. The app counts one country at a time. The months from August 2026 are near-real-time data without the FIRMS source label and are marked as preliminary. A single early month is a rough estimate; yearly totals and the season shape are more reliable.

DEMO VIDEO

The 30-second demo is a recording of the real app. Its narration voice is AI-generated (ElevenLabs text to speech) from a script written for the video. The opening picture is a real NASA VIIRS image and the music was synthesized with ffmpeg. No AI-generated images or video.

TOOLS

JavaScript without a framework, Node.js for data preparation, Leaflet for the map, NASA GIBS for the basemap, Cloudflare for hosting. The statistics run in the browser. 36 automated checks, including a recount of every month from the raw FIRMS files for all 13 countries.

NEXT

Joining NOAA-21 to the same record, daily updates, more countries (adding one takes three commands).
